summary: Defines the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior, a building block of Differentiated Services for low delay, low jitter, and low loss by serving an aggregate at a configured rate. It obsoletes RFC 2598. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some traffic, like a voice call, cannot wait. This is a fast lane at a router where such packets get served promptly at a promised pace.

questions: what is the ef phb codepoint
how does ef bound delay and jitter
subtitle: A precise definition of a router's fast lane: serve marked packets at a configured rate, no matter what else is queued.

tldr.problem: Services that need low delay, low jitter and low loss need packets to meet short or empty queues at every router, but the original EF description was hard to test and gave no way to bound the delay of an individual packet.
tldr.mechanism: A node promises to serve the EF aggregate at a configured rate R, and two sets of equations bound how far actual departure times may drift from ideal ones: one for the aggregate (error term E_a) and one for individual packets (error term E_p).
tldr.outcome: RFC 3246 replaces RFC 2598 with a mathematically rigorous definition of the same behavior. It defines only the behavior of a single node, not a whole service.

today: RFC 3246 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2598. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What EF Is For
sections.content:
Routers that implement Differentiated Services use a codepoint in the IP header to pick a per-hop behavior (PHB), the specific forwarding treatment for that packet. This RFC defines one PHB, Expedited Forwarding (EF), as a building block for low loss, low delay and low jitter services. How to build whole services from it is outside its scope.

The RFC argues that the dominant causes of delay are fixed propagation delays on wide area links and queuing delays in switches and routers. Propagation delay is fixed by the topology, so delay and jitter are smallest when queuing delay is smallest. Jitter here means the variation between maximum and minimum delay. If queues stay short relative to the buffer space, loss is also kept low.

EF is not mandatory. A node is not required to implement it to be DS-compliant, but a node that claims to implement EF MUST conform to this specification. EF only defines the behavior of a single node; a Per-Domain Behavior specification may describe a collection of nodes.

This document replaces RFC 2598. The main difference is added mathematical formalism for a more rigorous definition of the same behavior.
sections.eli5: Waiting in line is what makes things slow. EF is a lane where marked packets almost never have to wait, so they get through quickly and smoothly.

sections.title: The Intuitive Idea
sections.content:
The intuition is simple: the rate at which EF traffic is served on an output interface should be at least a configured rate R, over a suitably defined interval, independent of how much non-EF traffic is offered to that interface.

Two difficulties make this hard to turn into a rule. First, it is hard to pick the timescale for measuring R: short timescales introduce sampling errors, long ones allow excessive jitter. Second, EF traffic cannot be served at rate R when no EF packets are waiting, and from outside the router it may be impossible to tell whether a packet is waiting or merely delayed by internal processing.

The RFC's answer is to compute an ideal departure time for each EF packet and bound how far the real departure may fall behind it. The departure time is when the last bit leaves the node. If the previous packet has already left, the ideal departure is the arrival time plus the time to send the packet at rate R (its length divided by R). If packets are queued, the ideal start depends on whether the scheduler is running late or early relative to the previous packet's ideal departure.
sections.eli5: Imagine a checkout lane that promises to scan items at a steady pace. To check the promise, you work out when each item should have been done and see how late it really was.

sections.title: The Formal Definition
sections.content:
A node that supports EF on interface I at configured rate R MUST satisfy two pairs of equations. The first pair describes the EF aggregate:

d_j <= f_j + E_a   for all j > 0   (eq_1)
f_j = max(a_j, min(d_j-1, f_j-1)) + l_j/R   (eq_2)

Here d_j is the actual departure time of the last bit of the j-th EF packet to depart, f_j is its ideal target departure time, a_j is its arrival time, l_j is its size in bits measured on the IP datagram (no lower layer overhead), and R is in bits per second. E_a is the worst-case deviation for the aggregate. The last bit includes any layer 2 trailer.

The second pair uses capital letters (D_j, F_j, A_j, L_j) and the error term E_p:

D_j <= F_j + E_p   for all j > 0   (eq_3)
F_j = max(A_j, min(D_j-1, F_j-1)) + L_j/R   (eq_4)

The difference is packet identity. In eq_1 and eq_2 the j-th packet to depart need not be the j-th to arrive, because of multiple inputs and internal scheduling. In eq_3 and eq_4 the j-th packet to arrive is tracked to its own departure, which allows a bound on the delay of an individual packet. These are two ways to characterize one device, not two modes of behavior.

A compliant node MUST be characterized by the range of R values it supports on each interface and the E_a it can meet. R may be line rate or less. It SHOULD also be characterized by E_p, which may be given as a worst case or as a function of R, or as "undefined". When arrivals on different inputs are too close to order, a random tie-break is acceptable for conformance testing.
sections.eli5: The rules write down a target finish time for every packet, then say a router may only be a little late against that target. One rule watches the crowd of packets, the other watches each packet by name.

sections.title: Error Terms, Delay, Jitter and Loss
sections.content:
E_a and E_p are figures of merit. A smaller E_a means the device serves the EF aggregate more smoothly at rate R over short timescales; a larger E_a means a burstier scheduler that meets R only over longer intervals. A lower E_p means a tighter bound on an individual packet's delay. Many input interfaces, or per-flow scheduling inside the EF aggregate, can raise E_p. E_p is typically greater than or equal to E_a.

If the total EF load for an output, summed over all inputs, is bounded by a token bucket of rate r <= R and depth B, the delay bound is D = B/R + E_p (eq_5). Because minimum delay is at least zero, D also bounds jitter. For a tighter jitter bound, E_p MAY be split into E_fixed + E_variable, where E_fixed is the minimum delay through the node.

For loss, the RFC admits that any device with finite buffers may have to discard packets under high enough load. Conformance is then tested off-line: packets that did not leave are treated as lost and removed from the arrival stream, and the equations are checked on the rest. Which packets are lost is out of scope, but those not lost MUST still conform. A node MAY also be characterized by a token-bucket operating region in which no EF loss from congestion occurs.
sections.eli5: The two error numbers say how sloppy a router is allowed to be. Small numbers mean a smooth, predictable lane, and from them you can work out the longest any packet could wait.

sections.title: Codepoint, Marking and Neighbors
sections.content:
Codepoint 101110 is RECOMMENDED for the EF PHB. Packets marked EF MAY be remarked at a DS domain boundary only to other codepoints that satisfy the EF PHB, and SHOULD NOT be demoted or promoted to another PHB by a DS domain. Packets of a single microflow within the EF aggregate SHOULD NOT be reordered in normal operation. When EF packets are tunneled, the tunneling packets SHOULD be marked as EF.

Other PHBs may run on the same node, but the equations MUST hold independent of the amount of non-EF traffic offered. If EF is implemented with something that allows unlimited preemption of other traffic, such as a priority queue, the implementation MUST include a way to limit the damage to other traffic, for example a token bucket rate limiter. Traffic above that limit MUST be discarded, and the maximum EF rate (and burst size if appropriate) MUST be settable by a network administrator.
sections.eli5: EF packets wear a special sticker, and nobody may swap it for a lesser one. The fast lane also has a speed limit, so it cannot squeeze out everyone else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To protect against denial of service, the edge of a DS domain SHOULD strictly police all EF-marked packets to a rate negotiated with the adjacent upstream domain, and SHOULD drop packets above it. If two adjacent domains have not negotiated an EF rate, the downstream domain SHOULD use 0 as the rate, meaning it drops all EF-marked packets.

Traffic conditioning at ingress to a DS domain MUST also ensure that only packets whose DSCPs correspond to an EF PHB on entry are marked with a DSCP that corresponds to EF inside the domain. This guards against denial-of-service and theft-of-service attacks that exploit DSCPs not covered by any traffic conditioning specification at an ingress interface but which map to EF inside the domain.
sections.eli5: A fast lane invites cheating, so the entrance has a guard. Only packets that are allowed in, up to the agreed amount, get to use it.

sections.title: Implementation Examples
sections.content:
The appendix is not normative. It notes that a priority queue is widely considered the canonical example of EF. A perfect output-buffered device with a priority queue for EF gives both a low E_a and a low E_p. The main limit on E_a is that an MTU-sized non-EF packet that has just begun transmission cannot be preempted, plus any non-preemptable queues before the physical interface. E_p depends mainly on the number of interfaces.

A weighted round robin scheduler typically cannot support R as high as link speed, because the EF rate is affected by the number of other queues and their weights, and it likely has a higher E_a than a priority queue. Hierarchical scheduling that schedules sub-flows within the EF aggregate gives non-FIFO service, so E_p may be higher, and "undefined" may be the most appropriate value.

A domain may provide multiple instances of EF, each characterizable by the equations. In a multi-level priority scheduler, an instance that is not highest priority can wait long periods and see large E_a and E_p; in a WFQ-like scheduler each instance is a queue served at a configured rate and the values can resemble those for a single instance.
sections.eli5: A router can build the fast lane in different ways. A strict priority queue is the quickest, and fancier schedulers trade some smoothness for fairness.

cells: Low E_a and low E_p in a perfect output-buffered device
Likely higher E_a; may not support R near link speed
E_p may be higher, possibly undefined
